text_fidelity_a: Holy Stone HS170 Predator Mini RC Helicopter Drone 2.4Ghz 6-Axis Gyro 4 Channels Quadcopter Good Choice for Drone Training This is a fun little drone and well worth the money. It's easy once you figure it out and know what does what. Flying indoors is a bit of a challenge until you get a hold of it but outdoors it zips around like a hummingbird. It has headless mode which makes controlling it easier but it beeps while in headless mode.  It does not have alt hold so it won't hover in one level spot so you stay fully engaged with this during flight. The battery gets about 6-7 minutes. It's so light that a strong breeze will effect it outdoors but it can hold its own quite well. The prop guards and feet are pretty good for cushioning any crashes. Overall a very inexpensive but well built drone that is just a lot of fun to fly.

I thought my nieces boy would totally get a kick out of this and had to surprise him with it.

Who know it would be his grandfather who would be wasting all those wonderful bubbles when Luca wasn't around????

The cool thing is using this at dusk because it has some crazy light effects. It is really rapid fire. My brother was playing with a mix that made the bubbles more stiffer or rubbery so they would last longer.

I don't expect this to last very long as the kids were rough playing with it. My niece thought maybe to just start adding some colorful duct taping to it to make the plastic parts more resilient. Especially the part that snaps together.

I'm not saying it isn't made really good. The kids have been play fighting with it and it has been dropped or tossed several times. On the lawn it is safe from breaking. If they take it to the driveway were worried.
They are only allowed to play with it on the lawn. When they first used it in the patio, they made a mess!

it was a fun mess and i totally loved it because, hey.. That is what a great kids toy is for!

Consider getting TWO so that the kids can have more fun. Heck... get four! The mess can be rinsed off easy with a garden hose. Oh, Google Bubble Soap Mix. You will be surprised how much fun this can be when you have an endless supply of Bubble mix!

Snap Circuits Classic SC-300 Electronics Exploration Kit | Over 300 Projects | Full Color Manual Parts | STEM Educational Toy for Kids 8+ 2.3 x 13.6 x 19.3 inches I got this kit for my 10 year old. We had been experimenting with kit electric motors, magnets and radios and everything ended up mixed in a box that he liked to play with, so there was interest in this type of toy.

The parts of this kit snap together on a clear plastic grid. The instruction book is a black and white center stapled pamphlet that can be challenging to decipher for builds that are more complex. My son liked building the simple circuit that included the motor with the fan. Many of the advanced plans are very similar.

The kit seems durable but not indestructable. My kids can be pretty rough on things so they have been using this kit with my supervision.

For most kids under 10, this is not the type of toy that they can play with on their own. I have my son use this toy at the dining room table. We check to make sure that all of the parts get back in their place when we are done.

This is an educational toy. My experience is that early exposure to learning experiences like this can shape interests later on in life.

I would have liked to have seen a description of what the various modules do to the electricity to make the magic happen.

If you have any specific questions please leave a comment and I'll try to get back to you as soon as I can.
text_fidelity_b: Snap Circuits Classic SC-300 Electronics Exploration Kit | Over 300 Projects | Full Color Manual Parts | STEM Educational Toy for Kids 8+ 2.3 x 13.6 x 19.3 inches

Even though this toy is targeted for a younger age group, I still felt like he'd appreciate it, and he does. He has several other Imaginext toys in the JW realm, too.

He loves the mark on its foot. It has a Fallen Kingdom logo, as opposed to the JW logo. (This actually surprised me, since he loves looking for the JP or JW on toys.)

The Resistance (The Dystopian Universe) This game is addicting and so much fun for ages 10+. The teenagers at the summer camp I run especially found it fun.

The short version of how it works: Everyone gets an identity (spy or resistance member). Spies get to see who the other spies are, resistance members are clueless. You take turns choosing people to go on missions hoping that you don't have a spy among your group. Everyone on that mission turns in a pass or fail card. The spies are trying to get missions to fail, and resistance members are trying to pass the missions. You have 5 mission rounds to battle it out.

The first round or two playing with new people is always pretty quiet and awkward, but once everyone catches on to how to play, and opens up the game becomes a blast! It's been a great ice breaker for us, and it's got the kids talking and making friends with each other. All while being deceitful, calling others out for being spies, but overall having fun!

It's definitely more fun the more people you have, but it's still playable with only 5.
text_fidelity_b: The Resistance (The Dystopian Universe)

text_fidelity_a: Faber-Castell Do-Art Dot a Design Animals For ages 6 and up. The set comes with 6 "design sheets" for kids to paint, but there are only 3 designs (koala, turtle, or dolphin). You get one sheet with only black-and-white lines for an older child to paint and dot. You also get that same design with the main colors pre-printed and you only need to add dots of paint to the white dots in the design. The kit also comes with: 8 acrylic paints (light blue, dark blue, green, yellow-green, yellow, orange, red, purple), 2 fine tip dotters, 1 medium tip dotter, 1 brush, sticky tac (keeps paper flat while painting), 2 cardboard frames with hangers, and instructions. Acrylic paints can dry out quickly, so you may need to add water to the paints to keep them from drying out. Acrylic paints can quickly dry onto clothing and not come out, so you'll want to wear a painting smock. Wash dotters, brush (and work surface) before the paint dries if you intend to reuse them. The "dotters" are foam rounds on the end of a handle, and they create somewhat raised paint dots on the design sheets. It's a fun idea with colorful paints, but it is kind of simple so probably for younger kids rather than teenagers or older.

Cheerson CX-10 Mini 29mm Diameter 4CH 2.4GHz 6 Axis Gyro RC Quadcopter UFO RTF Green I would recommend this drone as anyone's first drone, or as a cheap toy to keep in the office.

I've purchased several of these for the children in my family. The are small, light, and perfect for flying indoors. I've crashed mine several time from 8-10 feet up and they just fall about bounce off the ground. The basic-ness of this drone reinforces the skills needed to fly all drones at a very low entry cost. In this way you don't feel bad about trying things and crashing. The features are very basic with the only programmed/smart option is a flip. There is a sort of hidden option to unlock "acrobatic mode" (read the instructions to unlock) which is really just turning the sensitivity of the controller, but definitely a challenge for new flyers.

Once you master flying this little guy around jumping up to a bigger "smarter" drone is a piece of cake, and if anything goes wrong you have the fundamental skills to fly and land.

text_fidelity_a:
White Mountain Wacky Packages - 1000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle [[VIDEOID:bbf13e80bc0bb99a1834994a2f95588d]] I liked this puzzle. It's based on a print of compilation artwork by Charlie Girard, based on Topps' Wacky Packages trading cards. The puzzle contains dozens of pictures of these cards. An example is "Smoocher's Sticky Jam: for longer kisses," instead of Smucker's Jam. Another example is "Toad: Froggy's favorite for the cleanest frog in town. Bubble bath for toads," instead of Tide detergent.

This puzzle claims it's the World's Funniest Puzzle. I think that's a bit of an over-exaggeration, unless you're the type of person who really likes pranks like the snake in the nut can, shock candy bars, and whoopee cushions. This puzzle doesn't contain any of those classic gags, but that's the style of the humor in this print. And, it makes sense, because the Topps cards that this artwork is based on are from the 1960's and 1970's. Topps reissues them every year, but they're classic, older cards that are pictured in this puzzle.

The quality of this puzzle is awesome! The packaging is great. The pieces are big and sturdy, with high quality cardboard and a nicely-colored back. The pieces fit together snugly, so it's easy to tell if they fit or not. As you can see from my video, it's sturdy enough to pick up, which is rare in puzzles.

Pros:
+Excellent quality and manufacture
+Funny, old style humor
+Very nice pieces

Cons:
-Probably not actually the world's funniest puzzle
text_fidelity_b: White Mountain Wacky Packages - 1000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle

text_fidelity_a:
My Little Pony Equestria Girls Pinkie Pie Doll For the past few months, every trip we made to the big-box store involved a determined march through the toy section, looking to see if the Equestria Girls dolls were yet available. My 9 year old, who watched My Little Pony endlessly, and has already watched Equestria Girls more times that I want to count, was thrilled when the dolls were finally available! Her favorite doll, by far, is the Deluxe version of Rainbow Dash [[ASIN:B00CANI9RQ My Little Pony Equestria Girls Rainbow Dash Hairstyling Doll]] -- because of all that multi-colored hair. I think Pinkie Pie comes in a close second place -- again, because of all that hair. The other Equestria Girl dolls have smooth, straight hair, so Pinkie Pie's masses of pink curls are a little different and fun to play with. And her pink skin tone is a little less eerie than the purple and blue of some of the other dolls.

Pinkamena Diane Pie has sparkly eyeshadow and a "cutie mark" on her cheek, reflective of her virtue. Pinkie Pie's cutie mark consists of three balloons, and reflects her virtue of laughter. Her happy, chaotic spirit is reflected in her curly hair. There's not much in the way of accessories -- a plastic headband to tame all those curls, and a little pink hairbrush. There is only one item of clothing -- the skirt -- so I don't think that these dolls will be dressed and undressed much -- that real appeal is the hair. The boots are interchangeable, so we have switched the boots around on several of the dolls. I find the boots a little disturbing -- well actually the legs, because the doll legs end at the ankle, and the boots pop on to the ankle. Without the boots, the dolls are footless. Kind of creepy, but I guess it's better than having those teeny weeny little Barbie high heels all over the place. Pinkie Pie has a small hole in her upper back -- it's pretty well hidden under all of that hair -- but some of the other dolls come with butterfly (or angel??) wings that pop into the hole, so Pinkie Pie can borrow those wings if she's so inclined, since she too has a hole for attaching the wings. Each Equestria Girl doll also comes with a sheet of stickers and a little pamphlet -- but my daughter hasn't even looked at those, and I expect they'll end up in the trash soon. The long piece of hair is supposed to be the horse-tail, but it is odd that it has a different texture than the rest of Pinkie Pie's hair. As a mom, I thought that the hair could have been better done -- the plugs are sparse and separated, so if you don't pull Pinkie Pie's hair back just right, she looks like she just visited Hair Plugs for Men -- not pretty.

Pinkie Pie is a cute doll with a big pouf of brushable hair. Is she super high quality? Probably not. Will she be a cherished heirloom to pass down over the years? Who knows. But is she a fun plaything for an Equestria Girls fan? You bet.
text_fidelity_b: My Little Pony Equestria Girls Pinkie Pie Doll

text_fidelity_a: Nature Gift Store Kids Worm Farm Observation Kit Shipped with Live Worms I ordered this as a Christmas gift for my young daughter who is into all things worms, gardening, and composting. It estimated it would arrive December 5th, but it arrived a lot earlier. I think earlier shipping is always fine with the exception of live creatures. Being more than a month away, I was worried the worms wouldn't make it for the holidays. I contacted the seller right away to get tips on how to keep the worms alive and they were not helpful at all. I think I got a one or two sentence reply with no information. So I decided to do some research myself and I was able to keep them all alive without having to transfer them until the farm was opened on Christmas day. I kept them in the dark and a cool area of my house. I would take the cup out once a week to check on them. I'd water the soil a little every other week (just moist, not wet). I also set a couple carrot shavings, a torn up spinach leaf, and a broken egg shell on the top.  The worms did really well.  We transferred them as soon as she opened the farm.  The farm itself was disappointing in size and much smaller than I was expecting. It's more like the size of holding your two hands side by side. We plan to transfer them from the farm to her vermicompost bin in a few weeks.  She seems happy with the purchase, but overall I would not recommend this farm and would suggest creating your own with a little more research.
text_fidelity_b: Nature Gift Store Kids Worm Farm Observation Kit Shipped with Live Worms

text_fidelity_a:
WowWee - MiP the Toy Robot - White This is a four star product in many ways. But I'm giving it three due to the following factors...

Excellent build quality and hardware features. However, without some additional software and accessories this you won't see lasting use.

Hardware: you WILL need a phone or tablet to unlock the limited potential of this toy. The included gesture and sound functionality is too rudimentary (and yet also hard to acess consistently) for lasting interest. If you don't plan to provide access to a tablet or phone, get WowWee's robotic dog product instead. Although it is easy to set up an obstacle course or seesaw on your own, purpose-built accessories would go a long way towards providing a "fiction" for the toy to inhabit, as well as proven fun activities.

Software: the existing apps are very well made and provide a significant boost to the toys functionality. I'd say about 75%. However, most are of limited scope and soon become repetitive. The best feature is the ability to remotely drive the robot and also record its adventures. I'd like to see a feature that allows kids to rudimentarily program the robot (perhaps to interact with purpose built accessories) not just activate sounds and colored lights... I'd also like to see the toolset opened to adults (Lua scripting?) so that they can extend the functionality for Pre-K through K STEM learning.

I understand trying to hit price points is important. But this is either a $75 toy with a few $25 accessory kits, or a $125 toy all in. The existing package (while decent) is limiting the potential of the product.
text_fidelity_b: WowWee - MiP the Toy Robot - White

text_fidelity_a:
Logo Party Board Game "Logo Party" gives players the chance to guess famous logos in a variety of ways. Depending on what type of card you draw, you will try to have other players guess the logo by drawing the clues (like Pictionary), acting out the item (as in Charades), or describing the brand (like the old game show "Pyramid".) Players have twenty seconds to guess the brand from the clues provided. Each team has a token to move around the board and try to get to the end first by guessing more brands than the other team. The game includes a tablet for the drawing clues and a box to hold the cards during play and for storage. Unfortunately, the box is too small and the cards don't fit well.

The game is designed for four or more players divided into two teams. The recommended ages are listed as eight and up, but most eight-year-olds would be unfamiliar with many of the brands featured in the game. In fact, even older teens and adults won't know some of these brands. Also, I would call some of the items products and not brands. For example, one of the "brands" is Chicken McNuggets (as opposed to McDonald's.)

The game is somewhat fun, but would be much better with a large group of people. My family found it almost impossible to act out most of the brands, but it was funny to see people try to act things out like "Tupperware". With more people, I'm sure it would be even funnier.

Throughout the boards, there are spaces called, "Reveal It". When landing on this space, players from both teams try to guess a brand by looking at the logo. This is also how the winner is ultimately determined when teams reach the end of the game board. The timer that comes with the game doubles as a holder for these cards. The card starts out fully covered and then parts of the brand are slowly revealed. This is a clever idea, but it's hard to place the card in the holder without looking at. Also, it makes an annoying buzzing sound (like the sound of a small wind-up toy.) Because of the sound, we used a different timer during regular play and saved the timer for the "Reveal It" cards.

The game would be more fun for a large group of people. My family had some fun playing "Logo Party", but got bored after a while since some of the brands were unknown to some of the players and it was hard to act out the brands and actually get someone to guess them.
text_fidelity_b: Logo Party Board Game

text_fidelity_a:
Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective: Jack the Ripper & West End Adventures Standalone Game The predecessor to this game, Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective, is my all-time favorite game, and holds a high place on my game shelf despite being a “one and done” experience. Does this new iteration hold up to the high standard the previous game established?

To start with, the production value on this new version is heads and shoulders above the 2013 edition of SHCD that I own. The paper is printed on much nicer stock, the box is thicker and better designed to hold the contents, and the instruction manual in particular shows a great attention to detail that the previous edition lacked. I particularly like that in this edition, the solutions to each case are printed upside down in the back of the box, and that the solutions are encased in an envelope secured to each case book to prevent spoiling any aspects of the story with erroneous page turns.

Like the previous game, this “board game” is much more of a “choose your own adventure” story for you and your friends to solve. Each case is represented by a book, in which you’re given an introductory story, and then allowed free reign to investigate a variety of leads and allies to assist you in gathering information about whodunit. Once you think you know what’s happening, turn to the questions and find out what happened in this story – don’t worry, there are significant explanations and story to give closure to each case.

This is a stand-alone game, meaning that if you haven’t already played the original SHCD, you can purchase this with no strings attached. I don’t think I would recommend that for new players, however.

Jack the Ripper and the West End Adventures are quite different from what you get in the original game. In the original, there were some threads of story that remained from one case to the next, but in the new version, four of the cases are designed to be played campaign-style in an effort to solve the Jack the Ripper murders.

I’m sure that there will be many people out there who love the Jack the Ripper campaign - a set of four cases that are thematically tied together that will allow you to hunt down Jack using a separate map and additional investigative helpers – but it really isn’t for me. First of all, the cases are quite a bit darker and less whimsical than your traditional Sherlock Holmes story and case, and are tied together only by the fact that they occur in the same area and time period. I think the original cases are too difficult to be played by, let’s say, a 10 year old, but the stories wouldn’t be inappropriate for them in terms of language and description. The Jack cases, on the other hand, would carry a definite R-rating – they’re well-researched historically, and include lots of graphic description and a few cuss words as well. If you know anything about the historical Jack cases, you’d probably know this going in, but if you’re used to the style of the original cases, know that this is a darker affair. Secondly, you absolutely cannot find Jack and get a satisfactory conclusion until the fourth case, which is a decent investment in time with little return for parts 1 - 3. Third, and this is the big reason I didn’t like it, is that the mini-mysteries you’re solving in parts 1, 2 and 3 are not mysteries at all, but historical backstory. The questions are answered directly by particular sources, so if you visit the right allies and pursue the right leads you will simply be given the correct answers to each piece without putting much of anything together outside of remembering what the leads gave you. This was a very different experience, with a different writing style, different thematic elements, and a wholly different style, and since I am such a fan of the tried-and-true SHCD formula, I did not enjoy it as much as others may.

The other six cases are all stand-alone cases, and are quite good, although in most cases, they’re quite a bit harder than the already difficult cases in the original box. Like that set, some are better than others, but I will admit that the overall quality of these cases is on-par with what came in the original box, but still harder. I don’t think this is the right place to start with the SHCD universe.

Therein lies the only real problem that I have with this SHCD set – that while packaged as a stand-alone, this game is put together in a way that strongly suggests that it’s a sequel. If you think of it in movie terms, sure, you can watch most sequels without seeing the original movies, but why would you, especially if you know going in that watching the original is going to improve your experience? The cases in this box are more difficult, and the Jack the Ripper set is an odd starting place.

Overall, this game comes very highly recommended to any fan of the original set of cases. If this game sounds like something you’d be interested in, get it, but be advised that I think that the original set of 10 cases are a superior starting place.

4.5/5
text_fidelity_b: Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective: Jack the Ripper & West End Adventures Standalone Game

text_fidelity_a:
7 Wonders We're a game playing family. With 84 board/card games and counting, I feel like something of an expert on board games. This was an exceptionally good game. Unlike some strategy games, there doesn't seem to be any one strategy that's going to always work. You have to be flexible, depending upon which wonder you end up with, the cards you get, and the strategies your opponents are using. You have to pay particular attention to the strategies of your nearest neighbors on either side because many actions and many cards play off of them. No cards or actions play directly off of an opponent who is not your neighbor. That, too, is a nice feature. It's not that you shouldn't watch what the people across the table are doing, but it's more important to know what the guys to the right and left are doing. Especially when you're dealing with higher numbers of players, that makes it easier to keep up with. That's a big part of why it works as well for 7 players as it does for 3. That, and the fact that game play is simultaneous -- no turn taking! So there's very little down time and the games moves quickly.

The only reason I didn't give this game 5 stars is that the game comes with rules for a 2-player variation that I do not believe is very good. I was hoping that this would be a game I could play with my husband after our (young) kids went to bed, but after trying several times we both agreed on two things:

1) There are much better 2-player games.
2) This game is much better with 3-7 players.

For those reasons, we will only pull it out when we have friends over. But it really, really is a top-notch game for the right number of players. I mostly wrote this review to caution people who are considering buying it more for it's two-player extendability than anything else.
text_fidelity_b: 7 Wonders

Melissa & Doug Folding Princess Castle Santa brought this princess castle for my 5 year old. She nearly went nuts when she saw it! Both her and her older sister constantly play with it. It's now 3 days after Christmas and they still both love it. Usually after the initial fun wears off (in a few hours) their toys sit unplayed with but not this castle.

It's exactly what you see in the picture. It's big and has lots of rooms, even a dungeon (of sorts) that constantly stir the imagination. Sturdy wood construction, elegantly painted, it's quite a toy. I wish I had one when I was a kid! I also bought the Princess Disney characters others have mentioned instead of the Melissa & Doug characters and they work wonderfully with the castle. I agree that the rooms are small, but I didn't buy this as a doll house for the girls to load up with furniture and pretend it's a real house.....it's a castle with a pretend moat, and dragons and shining knights in armor, and beautiful princesses and evil witches and all those imaginary things which make this castle so much fun to play with!

Also, it's extremely easy to put together. The only things you have to attach are the two towers and the connecting bridge. It arrived very quickly in the mail and was well packaged. I think it's worth the money and I'm about as cheap-minded as they come!

UPDATE: It's July 27, 2009 (7 months after purchase) and the girls both still love this castle. They play with it on an almost daily basis and it's currently set up in their bedroom floor with all sorts of necessary items around and inside of it. It seems to continually stir their imaginations.

text_fidelity_a: SUSSED The Weird Would You Rather Card Game | Ages: Teens, Adults, Kids 12+ | 110 Cards | for Family, Friends and More | Fantasy Version Played a quick round with my wife and 6-year-old daughter as soon as it arrived.  The game is quick and easy - a scorepad, a deck of cards, and a basic set of rules.  You ask questions, on mostly random subjects, and each of the two guessers attempts to figure out what the third player is going to choose from a set of 3 options.  The vocabulary and topic selection is a little tough for a bright 6-year-old, but a little rewording from Mom and Dad helped her get through it.  Overall, it's a cute idea, but it might get old quickly with only one deck, and it has minimal replay value, as the conversation quickly turns to "I would have chosen..." which is going to deflate your desire to play through multiple times.  There's not as many questions as you'd like to see since each card has 4 questions and that constitutes a round.  I could see a game like this making a nice icebreaker for a corporate team-building retreat or a get-to-know-your-classmates style game, but for a family game, it was good, not great, and not something that we'll likely keep coming back to.
text_fidelity_b: SUSSED The Weird Would You Rather Card Game | Ages: Teens, Adults, Kids 12+ | 110 Cards | for Family, Friends and More | Fantasy Version

Learning Resources 2-Color Desktop Abacus, Red Frame, Color Coded, Math Concepts, Ages 5+ This is a great abacus! I purchased this to help in our homeschooling math lessons and the kids love it!

Here's what I liked:
- The size - It fits perfectly on top of their school books and doesn't take up a ton of extra space.
- The groups of 5 beads - This is a good visual reminder that numbers can easily be split by 5s. (8 is 5+3)
- Sturdy frame - The red frame is not only easy to find but it is thick and very sturdy.
- Metal slides - Metal surpasses wood on nearly every level. The beads slide easily and we don't have to worry about breaking or getting splinters.
- Place value guides - These guides make it easy to visually show how place values work.

I would recommend this abacus for any child who prefers hand's on learning (Kinesthetic Learners) or even Visual Learners.
text_fidelity_b: Learning Resources 2-Color Desktop Abacus, Red Frame, Color Coded, Math Concepts, Ages 5+

text_fidelity_a:
Bezier Games One Week Ultimate Werewolf "Werewolf" games from Bezier games are becoming a bit ubiquitous at this point. That said, the core gameplay of the original, and certain spinoff titles like Inquisition have worked well for me in the past. "One Night" never really floated my boat, as it was too short and chaotic, so the "One Week" version seemed like a good fit.

In this game, you're moving around a castle board searching for Werewolves. You can do many "One Night" things - switch tokens without knowing who you are or who you become, and you need to bluff about which cards you are using. Unfortunately, this game shares a little too much from many of the same flaws that I noticed with One Night Ultimate Werewolf - it's too chaotic, it's still too quick, and you still will struggle to make strategic decisions because you don't often know what you are doing when you take actions. For people who enjoy the strategy-less designer games, like Talisman or traditional Werewolf, then this might be a hit if you have the right group.

For the right group, this will be a big success. While I do like it more than "One Night", it's not quite ready for my tastes yet.
text_fidelity_b: Bezier Games One Week Ultimate Werewolf

Mattel Games Pictionary: Frame Game I was really excited about this product, as Pictionary is one of my all-time favorite party games. This was a disappointment on so many levels.

First, there is no storage box. It comes with a frame, a frame stand, a timer, and a marker. And a dice, which got lost in no time. The "frame" itself is about the size of a sheet of paper (8" by 10"), and it is clear, so you can see through it. The small size makes it ideal for travel or a backpack, but the fact that it is clear makes it difficult to see when holding it on your lap. And forget about using it on the black coffee table. It works much better when used flat, on a light background surface. I like that you can use the frame as a window, so the see-through feature may be useful one at a time. It's pretty much impossible for two people to write on opposite sides of the board at the same time. Honestly it is pretty much for anyone to write on the board when it is in the stand, which keeps the board vertical.

We like to use large dry-erase boards when we pay Pictionary. I would recommend that rather than this game. The frame might be fun to draw on once in a while -- but shy not get a small whiteboard, which is much better suited for the purpose?
text_fidelity_b: Mattel Games Pictionary: Frame Game

We had a good talk and I had another student go to my room and get a hard sleeve card case (which we were also selling at the fundraiser) for him to put it in to protect it. I can see him putting it in his pocket and bending it and couldn’t stand the thought. He promised to take it home and not bring it back. I told him I know he would want to show his friends the card and now that he’s not allowed to bring it to school they may not believe him so I told him if anybody questioned him to come see me and I can let them know I seen it in person. text_fidelity_a:
Winning Moves Games Sorry Classic Edition Board Game, Multicolor My first introduction to the board game of Sorry was in the early 60's. Sorry was one of the more fast and fun games. The object of the game is to be the first player to move all 4 of your men around the board to get back home. You choose from 4 different colors of your men and your home- blue, green, yellow or red. There is a deck of cards that tell you how many spaces to move your man, and of course it isn't as easy as just moving your man as quickly as you can around the board to get home before anyone and win the game. There are obstacles along the way, should a player get to slide, he slides everyone in his way back to start, and no two men can occupy the same space, so someone has to go back to start- Sorry!

I remember when we played with 2 players, the game took about 15-20 minutes, but with 4 players, it took close to half an hour. It's very fast moving and even faster when hardly any players are sent back to start. I really love the look of this classic 1939 Sorry Game- it's a little different from the one we played on in the 60's. Regardless of the look you like, Sorry is a fast and fun game that brings back so many fun memories of when we had 15 minutes to kill before we went bike riding to a picnic on a lovely summer day in 1962. This early version of the game is really a nice one to own and it also comes with other game versions you can play including a Sorry For One, in case you have a few minutes to kill by yourself! Some Classic games never wear out their fast fun and this 5 Star Classic Sorry Board Game is one of them!
text_fidelity_b: Winning Moves Games Sorry Classic Edition Board Game, Multicolor

text_fidelity_a:
PlayMonster Farkle Frenzy Multi/None, 2 - 4 Player I looked forward to playing this game, but was very disappointed. It sounds fun - each player rolls five dice and adds their roll to the roll of a common die. I thought it would be more like Yahtzee, but it was not nearly as fun as that classic game. The common die gives the chance for each player to double their score, which helps someone come from behind and catch up with the player that is leading. However, when rolling only 5 dice, the odds of getting a decent roll were slim. It was almost impossible to get anything more than a three of a kind, and that was hard to do. This made the game more frustrating than fun. I've never played the original Farkle, and we had to make some house rules because many portions of the instructions were unclear, which added to my frustration. The instructions referred to online video directions being available, but I didn't think it was worth having to watch a video to learn to play what should have been a very simple dice game.

For those familiar with Farkle, the common die may add an interesting twist, but the bubble-popper and dice risers are unnecessary. The bubble-popper for the common die does not roll the die well and seems like it would break after a few uses. We took the die out and rolled it by hand. This was much easier and kept the game moving more quickly. (On a side note, when we removed the die from the bubble-popper, it looked dirty!) The dice risers are rickety and make the play of the game more confusing. Since you can't combine the numbers you get on individual rolls, it's necessary to keep track of what you got on each roll within a round. It was impossible to do this on the risers, so we just started putting the dice aside from each roll and not using the risers at all.

The dice themselves are sturdy, even though the white coloring started coming off the numbers after only a couple of uses. I like that there are four sets in different colors so each player can have their own color. However, the red and orange were too similar in color and it was hard to tell them apart.

Overall, I think the dice risers and bubble-popper are flimsy and just a gimmick to make more out of the game than there is. It's not an exciting game and became very boring when it became clear it was too hard to get a decent score from an individual roll.
text_fidelity_b: PlayMonster Farkle Frenzy Multi/None, 2 - 4 Player

Neo Pixel Light Saber, 20 Light Effects & 17 Sound Fonts Changeable, 41inch Smooth Swing Metal Hilt Light Saber Toys for Boys Girls, Gifts for Boysfriend, Dueling Light Sabers for Cosplay The Lorsaberus Lightsaber is nice looking and well made. As a die hard Star Wars Fan this Saber has a lot going for it, but a few cons. First the build and look are nice. The sound is also very good. The price is one of the best reasons for getting one. As of today a 40% off coupon making it around $72.00. To me at this price point shows you how much Disney and Star Wars The Black Series is ripping people off.

For the $72.00 you're getting 12 Light Sabers "colors" compare that to $250.00 and higher for one color. Now for the cons the blade is held in place by three set screws and it still has a bit of a lose feeling not much but its there. The other thing is the control button it is a bit cumbersome and by that I mean the holding down or pushing or doing the fast twist while holding button down to change sound fonts. I know some other saber makers use similar features but not this hard to change. One of the sound fonts is not even from Star Wars. I did not know what it was and could not stand it, but you might like. The problem was it took me several tries to change it and it should not be that hard to change.

So even with those two minor faults, this is still a great Saber for the price. As someone who was 10 years old when Star Wars came out, even now holding this and turning it on makes me smile.

"May the Force be with You"

Mega Construx Pokemon Detective Pikachu Hi-hat Café Construction Set with character figures, Building Toys for Kids (328 Pieces) Mega Construx blocks are compatible with LEGO brand blocks, but they have a different focus. In general, they focus on looking nicer, having smaller pieces with smooth edges, and are much more difficult to turn into an off-script creation. Also, they tend to have terrible instruction books, and this kit is no different.

The assembly requires a bit of imagination and guessing, and the kit is not packaged particularly well, as it often requires opening many bags at once to remove the singular small pieces referenced in the manual. Because of this, the kit is harder to assemble than your average LEGO set, but I have to admit that it looks pretty cool when it's done. There are not nearly as many LEGO pegs sticking out as you get on a typical LEGO build, and the figures articulate quite a bit more naturally.

Overall a fun kit for slightly more patient and experienced builders.
text_fidelity_b: Mega Construx Pokemon Detective Pikachu Hi-hat Café Construction Set with character figures, Building Toys for Kids (328 Pieces)
